subject: Urban Planning
title: Minimum Lot Sizes: Pricing Out by Acreage
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Minimum Lot Sizes: Pricing Out by Acreage.

hook.text: Some suburbs require one-acre minimum lots. That means the cheapest possible home needs $300,000 worth of land.

buildup.text: Minimum lot sizes were designed to keep suburbs exclusive. Larger lots mean higher costs and fewer homes.

discovery.text: In Connecticut, some towns require two-acre minimums. A modest home on that land costs $800,000 before building starts.

twist.text: Large lot zoning is race-neutral on paper but exclusionary in effect. It prices out anyone below upper-middle class.

climax.text: New Jersey's Mount Laurel doctrine requires every municipality to zone for affordable housing. It's been resisted for 50 years.

punchline.text: Require an acre per house. Keep out everyone who can't afford it. Call it 'character.'

quiz.question: How do minimum lot sizes create economic exclusion?
options: They require expensive landscaping that raises maintenance costs
They force higher land costs per home, pricing out lower-income buyers
They mandate underground utility connections that add building costs
